lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r1s0 (improvement, +751.57%): Combinational `/` and `%` in the single-cycle ALU set a ~200 ns critical path (5.44 MHz) that every instruction paid for, even though CoreMark's timed region almost never divides, so a 32-cycle radix-2 sequential divider that stalls IF/ID gave ~8.5x fitness with negligible IPC loss; the 33x33 multiplier was not critical and could stay single-cycle, and deriving `ex_busy` only from flops (ID/EX is_div & ~div_done) kept the stall off the new ~27 ns redirect->IF->hazard->flush_id path.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r1s1 (regression, +702.23%): Moving MUL into the multi-cycle M-unit along with DIV/REM scored 97.23 iter/s, below the 103.21 of the divider-only sibling hyp-001; once the combinational `/`/`%` is gone, the single-cycle 33x33 DSP multiply is not on the critical path (hyp-001 reached 46.4 MHz with it in place), so multi-cycling it most likely bought no Fmax and only added 2-3 stall cycles per MUL in core_matrix, which means a unit should only come off the EX path when the timing report shows it is critical.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r1s2 (regression, +5.94%): The fetch-stage 64-entry BTB + bimodal + 4-entry RAS was built on the old core, where the ~200 ns combinational-divider path (5.44 MHz) still set the clock, so it could only win IPC; it scored 12.84 vs the 12.12 baseline, about half the predicted +11% and far below the 103.21 of its divider-fix sibling hyp-001, so if Fmax stayed divider-bound it recovered only ~6% of cycles, which means taken-branch bubbles are a much smaller share of CoreMark cycles than the assumed 15-18% (or the predictor hit rate is poor); re-porting it onto the divider-fixed core is worth ~+6% only if the new PC -> LUT-RAM BTB -> tag compare -> next-PC path and the EX mispredict-compare -> IF path stay under the ~27 ns critical path, because at ~46 MHz a path into u_if/pc through u_hazard is already the critical path in hyp-002.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r2s0 (regression, +42.00%): Cutting both tied ~26.8 ns cones in one change scored 146.56 vs the 103.21 champion (about 66 MHz if cycles are unchanged, as designed, which matches the estimated ~15 ns path); the four cycle-neutral cuts were a dedicated rs1+imm AGU registered as EX/MEM mem_addr (Gowin pulls that flop into the dmem BSRAM address register, so the address pins otherwise see the whole ALU/DSP cone), feeding the multiplier from post-forward rs1/rs2 with its output at the last mux level before EX/MEM, dropping the IF NOP-on-redirect so branch resolution no longer feeds IF/ID -> load-use -> flush, and narrowing the ID/EX bubble to valid plus side-effect ctrl bits; the "regression" tag most likely only means a sibling ranked higher, and together with hyp-002 r1 (capped at 45.5 MHz by the untouched redirect->u_hazard path) it shows that tied critical cones have to be fixed in the same iteration.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r2s1 (improvement, +46.70%): This had the same AGU, late-MUL, redirect-off-IF and narrow-flush cuts as hyp-001 r2s0 plus extra ID precompute (forward flags registered from ID-stage rd compares and gated in EX by the producer's registered reg_write, which is exact because ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB capture on the same !dmem_stall && !ex_busy && !load_use cycles; LUI/AUIPC/link pre_result; one-hot result-lane selects), yet it scored only ~3% more (151.41 vs 146.56, roughly 68 vs 65.8 MHz at unchanged cycles), most likely because r2s0's new critical path already ran regfile BSRAM -> bypass -> forward mux -> 32-bit branch compare -> redirect -> u_if/pc (16 levels), and registered selects only remove the rd compares from that path, so the next Fmax step must shorten branch resolve -> PC itself (e.g. an ID-side compare or a registered redirect) rather than split EX lanes further.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r2s2 (regression, +4.97%): Porting the 64-entry BTB + bimodal + 4-entry RAS onto the divider-fixed hyp-001 core, with EX mispredict driving only the PC mux and a registered squash_q killing the single wrong-path fetch, scored 108.34 vs 103.21, close to the +7% forecast (if cycles fell ~6.8% as in r1s2, Fmax slipped only ~2% to ~45.4 MHz), so the predictor's IPC gain survives timing when the redirect tail is flop-cut; it lost only because its same-round sibling r2s1 reached 151.41 at ~68 MHz from the same base, so the ~5% should be rebased onto r2s1, where the EX branch-compare -> mispredict -> u_if/pc path is already the ~14.7 ns critical path and the pred.taken/tgt_ok terms and the pred_target/correct_pc next-PC mux must add no logic levels to it.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r3s0 (regression, +17.81%): Forcing the regfile out of BSRAM (distributed RAM, bypass resolved in ID, written-valid vector instead of a reset loop) so the ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val flops are no longer absorbed as the BSRAM read register scored 178.38, about 80 MHz at unchanged cycles and at the top of its 76-80 MHz forecast, which confirms that the ~3-4 ns BSRAM tC2Q + bypass-LUT prefix shared by all three tied EX cones was the Fmax limiter; it lost by only ~0.6% to sibling r3s1 (+18.5%), which also moved the whole forward mux into ID, so where the forward mux sits and this entry's MUL-from-rs2 and one-hot branch-select tail trims were worth at most about 1% together, and the next step needs a fresh timing report on r3s1 rather than more EX-tail trimming.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r3s1 (improvement, +18.51%): Moving the whole forward mux into ID (async LUT-RAM regfile read, EX > EX/MEM > MEM/WB > regfile priority, late `ex_result` at the last LUT before the ID/EX flops, so every EX lane starts from a plain flop) is the new champion at 179.43, but it missed its +25-30% forecast (the cycle time fell from 15.6 ns to about 13.2 ns, not the predicted 9.5-11 ns, assuming cycles are unchanged as designed) and beat sibling r3s0, which kept the mux at the start of EX, by only ~0.6%; the most likely reason is that the forward mux sits on the single-cycle back-to-back loop (ALU/MUL lane -> forward -> dependent operand) whichever side of the ID/EX flop it is placed, so moving it only helps the non-feedback branch and AGU cones, while ALU/MUL -> `ex_result` -> forward LUT -> ID/EX still carries it, which means a timing report should check whether that loop is now the limiter, and if it is, the ALU/MUL lane itself must get shorter (e.g. forward MUL only from EX/MEM behind a one-cycle mul-use interlock) rather than the operand side being restructured again.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r3s2 (regression, -7.07%): The zero-bubble decode-time JAL + BTFN-agree bimodal predictor delivered the cycle cut its ISS bubble count forecast (140.70 iter/s at 59.1 MHz implies ~4.20M cycles, -6.5% vs 4.49M), but Fmax fell from 68.0 to 59.1 MHz (-13%) even though the new worst path (regfile -> ALU -> alu_result, 22.3 ns vs the champion's 20.97 ns) contains no predictor logic, so the most likely cause is placement pressure from +385 LUT / +277 FF (a 256-flop counter table with a second read port for EX/MEM training, plus a dedicated pc+imm adder) on a ~2.4k-LUT core whose EX cones are tied; ISS bubble counts are therefore a trustworthy cycle forecast, but a ~6-7% IPC gain leaves almost no Fmax budget (it must lose less than ~2% to clear the 4.6% bar), so a retry should first cut the area (counters in LUT-RAM or carried down the pipe for a single read port, 64 entries) and be rebased onto the 80.6 MHz r3s1 champion.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r4s0 (improvement, +31.15%): Cutting all three tied ~11.7 ns cones in one change is the new champion at 235.32 vs 179.43, more than twice its +13% forecast. The three cuts were: registering the full 64-bit DSP product into EX/MEM.mul_p on the !stall enable, with MEM picking the half and a registered ID/EX late_result = mem_read | is_mul folding MUL into the load-use interlock; flat one-hot ALU lanes with ID-decoded selects in place of the case-over-op plus AND-OR; and one-hot load byte selects decoded in EX with the load value moved to the last forward level. If cycles rose only the designed ~1%, this implies about 106-107 MHz vs 80.6, which confirms r3s1's diagnosis that the single-cycle ALU/MUL -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop was the limiter, and it shows that a pipelined MUL behind a one-cycle mul-use interlock is cheap once the DSP is critical (unlike r1s1's 2-3-cycle multi-cycle MUL); the branch-compare -> PC and AGU -> BSRAM paths evidently sat well below the ~11.4 ns the forecast assumed, so the next step needs a fresh timing report to find the new limiter.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r4s1 (regression, +14.04%): This used the same three cuts as its same-round sibling r4s0 (raw 64-bit DSP product registered into EX/MEM.mul_p behind a late_rd = mem_read | is_mul interlock, flat ID-selected ALU lanes, registered load byte-lane selects with load_data at the last forward level) and landed inside its own 90-95 MHz forecast (about 92.6 MHz if cycles match r4s0's 4.53M), but that is about 15% below r4s0's 106.5 MHz, a larger gap than r4s0's own ~9% place_option spread (97.7-106.5 MHz), so the plan itself is confirmed and the gap most likely comes from RTL detail inside the single-cycle EX -> ex_result -> forward loop (the visible candidate is r4s1's shift lane, a 33-bit SRA plus a separate SLL behind a shift_right mux), which is unverified without a timing report, so follow-ups should build on r4s0's RTL, not r4s1's.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r4s2 (regression, +5.60%): The low-area retry of r3s2's zero-bubble decode predictor (JAL + BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM counters with a single sync write port trained only from EX/MEM flops, IF's predicted next PC taken from id_stage's existing pc+imm adder, EX checking direction only with the redirect kept at the last next-PC mux level) scored 189.47 vs 179.43, close to its +7% forecast, which implies about 79.6 MHz (only ~1% below 80.6) if cycles fell to r3s2's ~4.20M, so it confirms that r3s2's -13% Fmax came from area/placement pressure and not from the prediction policy; it most likely lost only to sibling r4s0 (235.32 at ~106.5 MHz), and a rebase onto r4s0 must re-check timing first, because the fetch-side flop -> imm_gen -> pc+imm carry chain -> pred mux -> u_if/pc path was estimated at 7-9 ns, which is close to r4s0's ~9.4 ns period rather than safely under the old 12.4 ns.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r5s0 (regression, +1.43%): Cutting all three tied ~10.2 ns cones that filled the whole top 25 was forecast at +9-12% but scored only 238.68 vs 235.32; the cuts were a one-LUT branch resolve into a registered sel_q/tgt_q/seq_q PC select, a one-LUT5 ex_result with pre_result forwarded from its ID/EX flop and DIV moved behind the late-result interlock, imm loaded into ID/EX.rs2_val in place of the alu_b mux, and MUL sign bits built in EX; if cycles rose only by the DIV-use bubble this is about 108 vs 106.5 MHz, well inside the ~9% place_option spread, so a fourth cone that the saturated report never showed was almost tied with the three, and the likely candidates are the compare -> cond -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl sync-RESET fan-out, which still carries lt/eq (10.085 ns in the old report), and the load extract -> forward path; when tied cones fill the entire timing report, get a deeper report (more paths, or the worst path per endpoint group) before forecasting any gain past the reported cones.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r5s1 (regression, -7.94%): The bypassed 2-entry prefetch queue cut cycles as forecast (4.37M vs 4.53M, -3.5%), and the one-LUT redirect plus pre-muxed alu_b took the branch -> PC cone out of the top paths, but median Fmax fell from 106.5 to 94.7 MHz (+111 LUT); the most likely cause is that the queue-empty bypass put the raw io_imemReady input and a head/bypass mux level in front of the whole ID cone (instr select -> decoder/imm_gen -> pc+imm -> pre_result, and -> forward selects -> rs2_val), which became a new ~10.1 ns cone tied with the shamt -> shifter -> ex_result -> forward loop, and the implementer's place_option 0 check (98.33 vs 97.65 MHz, +0.7%) did not show the loss, so a decoupled front end should keep imem_ready off the instr/decode bits (let it gate only the ID/EX valid and side-effect ctrl bits, as in r2s0's narrow flush), and Fmax should be compared with the champion's median across placement options, not with option 0 alone.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r5s2 (regression, +2.76%): Rebasing r4s2's low-area decode predictor (JAL + BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM, predicted target from id_stage's pc+imm) onto r4s0 with a registered 2-cycle mispredict redirect (redirect_q/target_q flops as the top PC priority, the wrong-path EX slot killed through valid/ctrl-only EX/MEM clears, flush_id = redirect_q || load_use) scored 241.82, the best entry of round 5 but only about half its +5-7.5% forecast; if cycles reached the forecast ~4.30M, this implies about 104 MHz, ~2% below r4s0's 106.5 MHz median, so taking the branch compare off the paths into u_if/pc and flush_id gained no Fmax (as in r5s0, which also cut that cone and reached only ~108 MHz), most likely because the ALU/shift -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop still caps the clock, while the ~+150 LUT predictor, or its new LFSR -> imm_gen -> pc+imm -> pred mux -> pc fetch path, cost the same ~1-2% that r4s2 paid; the predictor's gain should therefore be counted as IPC only, net of ~2% Fmax, and stacked on a core that shortens the ALU loop rather than justified by removing the branch cone.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r6s0 (regression, +1.26%): Cutting all four tied cones in one change was forecast at +6-9% but scored 238.28, level with r5s0's 238.68 (about 108 MHz at ~4.53M cycles). The cuts were a 2-LUT branch resolve into a pc_d mux, an explicit 4:1/4:1/2:1 shifter with separate SLL and SR lanes, a one-LUT5 ex_result with DIV behind the late-result interlock, and imem_ready moved off the instr/regfile-address bits with x0 folded into the forward select code. Two rounds that each cut every reported cone by 2-3 LUT levels have now stalled at the same ~108 MHz, inside the ~4-9% place_option spread, so counting LUT levels per cone no longer predicts Fmax on this core. The remaining limit is most likely route delay on high-fanout flops (rs1_val fanout 14 with a ~2.8 ns route, sub fanout 33) and the carry chains in the single-cycle EX -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop, not logic depth. The next Fmax step therefore needs a structural change, such as duplicating the high-fanout operand flops or breaking the forward loop with an ALU-use bubble, or else a timing report on r6s0 that shows a new limiter.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r6s1 (regression, -6.79%): This rebuilt r5s1's 2-entry fetch queue as a shift register whose flop-selected q0/imem_data head mux replaced the NOP mux, so imem_ready reached only valid and the narrow ID/EX flush, and it added r5s0-style ALU/MUL loop cuts, but it scored 219.34 vs 235.32; if cycles again fell to r5s1's ~4.37M, that implies about 96 MHz, the same ~10% Fmax loss as r5s1 (94.7 MHz), while r6s0 took imem_ready off the ID read path without a queue and held ~108 MHz, so r5s1's imem_ready diagnosis was wrong and the cost belongs to the queue itself, most likely the 3-input head mux on every instr bit (unlike the 2-input NOP AND it replaced, it cannot fold into the downstream decoder/LUT-RAM-address LUT4s) and the pop/push enable, which depends on load_use computed from that same muxed instr and drives the CE of ~130 payload flops; a ~3.5% IPC gain cannot pay for that, so a fetch queue whose head feeds ID combinationally should not be tried again unless a timing report of the queue build shows these paths well off the critical path.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r6s2 (regression, -5.32%): Rebuilding r5s2's predictor with a shortened fetch path scored 222.81 vs r5s2's 241.82. The changes were a raw IF word with the imem-stall bubble moved into the narrow ID/EX flush, a separate instr[3:2]-selected B/J/U immediate in front of the shared pc+imm adder, and pc_imm moved to the last pc_d mux level. If cycles stayed at r5s2's ~4.30M as designed, this implies about 96 MHz vs 103.9, an ~8% Fmax loss where +1-2% was forecast. r6s0 made the same raw-IF-word/narrow-flush change on the same base and held ~108 MHz, so the loss most likely comes from the duplicate immediate decoder (a second load on every IF-word imm bit beside imm_gen, feeding an adder that also drives ID/EX.branch_target and the AUIPC pre_result) and the pc_d reordering. As with r6s1's queue head mux (also ~10% lost), extra logic hung on every IF-word bit costs more in route/fanout than the LUT level it saves, so the predictor should be kept exactly as r5s2 built it (shared imm_gen pc+imm, pred ? pc_imm : pc+4, redirect_q on top), and a reported worst path on this core should not be trimmed further unless a timing report on the new build confirms it is still the limiter.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r7s0 (regression, -9.52%): Acting on r6s0's route-delay diagnosis by splitting ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val into three lane-local copies (a_alu/b_alu with imm pre-muxed plus a separate sh_amt, a_cmp/b_cmp for compare and AGU, md_a/md_b for DSP/DIV/store data), each fed by its own last-level forward LUT, with per-byte `sub` copies and the load sign fill folded into the forward LUT, was forecast at +6-12% but scored 212.92, about 96 MHz vs r6s0's ~108 MHz if cycles stayed at the designed 4.53M; the most likely reason is that every copy needs its own forward LUT, so ex_result and load_data, the source nets of the single-cycle EX -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop and of the BSRAM load path, now drive three times as many LUTs spread between the ALU, the compare/AGU carry chains and the DSP column, which moves the long route from the operand flop onto the loop itself and adds ~130 forward LUTs and ~190 FFs of placement pressure; operand duplication should not be retried unless the non-ALU copies are taken off the single-cycle forward loop (e.g. forwarded only from EX/MEM behind an interlock) or the loop is broken with an ALU-use bubble, and any retry must first check the post-synthesis FF count and the worst path's routes to confirm the copies survived and to see where the long route moved.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r7s1 (regression, -12.63%): Unlike its sibling r7s0, this fed its syn_preserve lane-private ID/EX operand copies (A adder/compare, B shifter, C logic/AGU/MUL/DIV/store) and half-word select copies from one shared forward LUT per bit, which avoids the tripled ex_result/load_data loads that r7s0 blamed, and it carried over r6s0's cycle-neutral cuts, yet it scored 205.61, about 93 MHz vs r6s0's ~108 MHz at the designed ~4.53M cycles and even below r7s0's ~96 MHz; the most likely cause is that the ID/EX operand flop sits inside the single-cycle ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop, so replicating it only moves the long route from flop -> spread-out lanes to forward LUT -> copies placed at those lanes on the same flop-to-flop path (this build also hung a second 32-bit compare subtractor and a 32-bit eq on copy A, so A still fed three wide structures), which means both forms of operand-flop duplication (per-copy or shared forward LUT) have now lost 10-13%, the next Fmax step must break or shorten the loop itself (an ALU-use bubble, or forwarding non-ALU consumers only from EX/MEM), and any future replication must first confirm from the post-synthesis FF count that the copies survived (none was reported for this run).

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r7s2 (improvement, +7.09%): Rebuilding r5s2's decode predictor exactly (JAL + BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM, target from the shared imm_gen pc+imm adder) but with a direct 1-cycle mispredict redirect is the new champion at 252.01, just above its +5-7% forecast; if cycles reached the forecast ~4.23M, this implies about 106.7 MHz, level with r4s0's 106.5 MHz median, so the ~2% Fmax that r4s2 and r5s2 paid was not inherent to the predictor. The redirect stayed off r4s0's cone because ID folded pred, funct3 and the taken-target alignment into registered one-hot "redirect-when" flags (EX computes only flag & eq/lt/ltu ORed, plus f_jal and f_jr & !agu_sum[1]) and registered alt_target = pred ? pc+4 : pc+imm, so the EX target mux kept its is_jalr ? agu : flop shape. Together with r5s0, r5s2 and r6s0, this shows that on this core a registered redirect only adds a bubble per mispredict/JALR (~62k cycles) and buys no Fmax, so predictor-resolve logic should be pre-decoded into ID/EX flags rather than cut with an extra stage. The don't-care imm_gen (which removes load from IF-word bits, unlike r6s2's duplicate decoder that lost 8%) changed in the same build, so its share of the recovered Fmax cannot be separated. With ~51k direction mispredicts and 13.8k JALRs left (<1.5% of cycles), the predictor category is nearly exhausted, and the next gain has to come from Fmax, i.e. the ALU -> ex_result -> forward loop.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r8s0 (regression, -0.68%): Relieving the two largest late-arriving control fanouts without changing cycles scored 250.30 vs 252.01, about 106.0 vs 106.7 MHz if cycles stayed at the designed 4.23M, which is well inside the place_option noise. The three changes were: flush_id now clears only the ~16 side-effect bits (valid, reg_write, mem_*, is_div, is_branch/is_jump, late_result, f_* flags) instead of the whole ctrl struct and lane selects; load_use is off the CE of ~200 ID/EX data flops (stall_id_data = dmem_stall || ex_busy, so a load-use bubble captures stale don't-care data); and the pipeline data fields no longer have a sync reset. The reported compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl endpoint was therefore only one of many near-tied paths, and cutting control-net fanout or merging CE/SR control sets buys no Fmax on this core, just as trimming LUT levels bought none in r5s0/r6s0. With r7s0/r7s1, this leaves the single-cycle ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop as the likely ~106-108 MHz ceiling, and it must be broken (an ALU-use bubble, or EX/MEM-only forwarding for non-ALU consumers) rather than having load taken off its side nets.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r8s1 (regression, -3.46%): This build made three cuts. SLL/SR/SLT/DIV left the single-cycle EX -> ID forward merge (ex_fast = add | logic | pre, 2 LUT levels) and were forwarded from EX/MEM behind the late-use interlock. alu_b was pre-muxed in ID, which took the fanout-74 alu_src flop off the adder head. The redirect no longer drove flush_id, because a kill_q flop squashed the wrong-path slot in EX. It was forecast at +5% (113-116 MHz for ~2% more cycles) but scored 243.30 vs 252.01, which is about 105 MHz vs 106.7 if cycles rose as designed, so it gained no Fmax and the new shift/SLT-use bubbles were pure loss. The forecast ignored its own timing report: the untouched load-forward cone (dmem BSRAM DO -> ld_sign -> load_data -> rs1_fwd -> ID/EX, 9.437 ns) sat only 0.12 ns (~1%) behind the two 9.55 ns loops it cut, so the best case was ~1%. An Fmax forecast must therefore be capped at the next-worst untouched cone in the report, and cycles (new interlocks, lanes forwarded late) should be traded for Fmax only when that cone is several percent behind. On this core load_data enters the same forward LUT as ex_result, so no EX-side shortening of the forward loop can beat the load path unless that path is cut in the same build.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r8s2 (regression, +3.63%): The predictor-steered 16x32 LUT-RAM loop stream buffer cut CoreMark cycles by more than its -5 to -6.5% forecast (3.88M vs 4.23M, -8.3%), so imem backpressure hidden inside short predicted-taken backward loops is a bigger IPC lever than the <1.5% the predictor has left, but median Fmax fell from 106.7 to 101.3 MHz (-5%), so the net +3.6% missed the bar even though both siblings scored lower. The Fmax cost came from the IF word: the planned async buffer read in front of the IF-word mux put the LUT-RAM read at the head of the decode -> forward -> ID/EX cone (77 MHz at place_option 0), and reading the buffer one cycle early into a 32-bit word register recovered most of that, yet the flop-selected 2:1 mux on every IF-word bit, the imem-stall term folded into flush_id and ~+56 LUT / +36 FF still cost ~5%, while r6s0's raw IF word held ~108 MHz and the worst path stayed the old compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl cone, which points to route/placement pressure rather than a new cone. This is the third build, after r6s1's queue head mux and r6s2's duplicate immediate decoder, in which logic added on the IF-word bits cost 5-10% Fmax, so a fetch-side IPC idea should be forecast net of ~5% Fmax unless its substitute word avoids the IF-word -> decode path.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r9s0 (improvement, +7.88%): Rebuilding r8s2's loop stream buffer with the same replay policy but with the champion's IF-word and flush structure is the new champion at 271.88, at the top of its +6-8% forecast. If cycles again reached r8s2's ~3.88M, this implies about 105.5 MHz, only ~1% below r7s2's 106.7 and ~4% above r8s2's 101.3. Three things changed from r8s2. The IF word stayed a single LUT4 per bit on four flops (instr = hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP, where io_imemData/io_imemReady are bench flops and word_q is read one cycle early from a pc[5:2]-indexed LUT-RAM). The hit entered only as imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q, feeding stall_if and valid. flush_id and the redirect/PC mux were left byte-identical, and less bookkeeping area was planned. This shows that substitute-word logic on the IF word does not inherently cost the 5-10% Fmax seen in r6s1, r6s2 and r8s2: it is nearly free when it stays one LUT on early flops, the same depth as the NOP mux it replaces, and adds no input to the critical flush_id net. All three of r8s2's costs (the 2:1 mux replacing the NOP mux, the imem term on flush_id, and the extra area) were removed in the same build, so their individual shares cannot be separated, and it is unconfirmed whether the +40 LUT area target was met.

- 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r9s1 (regression, -19.25%): The 64-word direct-mapped L0 icache scored 203.49 vs the r7s2 base of 252.01, which implies about 79-86 MHz vs 106.7 if cycles landed between r8s2's 3.88M and the unchanged 4.23M (no cycle count was reported), a ~20-25% Fmax loss where -2 to -4% was forecast. Its IF word was always the word_q flop, and hit = tag_q == pc[19:8] gated only valid/stall_if/flush_id. The most likely cause is that its "read one cycle early" was indexed by the next PC: the build read the ins/tag arrays at every candidate next PC and applied the PC flop's redirect > stall > pred choice after the arrays. That put the late selects (EX compare -> redirect, IF word -> load_use -> stall_if, IF word -> pred) and the IF word -> imm_gen -> pc+imm -> LUT-RAM -> word_q loop in front of ~45 word_q/tag_q flops, multiplied the LUT-RAM read ports, and again folded the imem-stall term into flush_id as r8s2 did. The forecast's argument that the low index bits leave the carry chains early ignored that the mux selects arrive late.
